text: The weaver took over the family workshop because orders for blankets had dwindled to almost nothing. She learned the trade by stages: sorting fleeces first, then spinning, and at last weaving broad lengths of cloth. That slow apprenticeship left a mark on the way she works, for she can name a fibre by touch alone, without so much as a glance at it. Industrial dyes struck her as harsh, so she colours her skeins in baths of boiled roots and bark. No two vats give quite the same shade, and it is that very unevenness which draws customers weary of uniform cloth. Demand rose, and with it the need for help, so she took on an apprentice. The younger woman begins by learning to watch, since a thread pulled too tight will warp the whole piece. Patience, the weaver says, is no virtue here but a technical condition.

units: the speaker was disappointed by a knitted garment as soon as he put it on

drying had to be done flat and without wringing by hand
after that treatment the knit turned supple and downy

in his view no amount of care corrects a badly drafted pattern

text: That cardigan let me down the moment I tried it on. The knit felt scratchy, the collar rasped against my neck, and the wrapping had promised something soft as a cloud. I very nearly sent it back without a word. Then a friend who sews suggested a wash in lukewarm water with a splash of vinegar, followed by drying flat, never wrung out by hand. The change surprised me: the knit came out supple and almost downy, and the collar stopped prickling. Since then I pass the tip on to anyone grumbling about a rough jumper. My objection to the cut still stands, mind you. The sleeves hang too low, the shoulders gape, and no amount of washing rescues a badly drafted pattern. Put that right and the workshop would have an honest garment at a fair price. As things are, I wear it indoors and never past the front door.

units: the writer is writing from a place where clothes are repaired

text: I am writing from the alterations workshop, between fittings, because your question about shoes deserves a straight answer. You are torn between two fastenings: one shoe closes with a buckle, the other with laces. The buckle goes on in a single movement, which suits anyone heading out in a hurry. Laces make you sit down, pull them tight and check the tension across the instep, and in return they hold the ankle far better. Both kinds pass through my hands here. Buckles tend to give way at the rivet, and mending one costs a good deal more than a fresh set of laces. So if the ground underfoot is rough and broken, take the laced pair. If your day is a string of short errands, the buckle will serve. Write and tell me what you decide, for I have put aside a pair of each in your size.

units: the text asks what tells one material from another

the animal fibre offers a springiness that restores the shape
the most prestigious material makes those who speak of it fall silent
the most widespread fibre stirs little enthusiasm because it is ordinary
those who practise the trade know these materials with their eyes shut
text: What tells one cloth from another, if not the hand that judges it? The weaver answers by weight, the seamstress by how a piece holds its shape, the dyer by how greedily the fibre drinks. Each of them is right, and each says too little. Ask about linen and they speak of a dry coolness, of creases no iron ever quite smooths away. Ask about wool and they describe a warmth that breathes, a spring that carries the knit back to its shape. Ask about silk and their voices drop, as though the word on its own were enough. And cotton? It stirs no poetry, because it turns up everywhere and slips out of mind. There lies the riddle of these materials: they yield to description through their uses, never through their nature. Whoever handles them long enough comes to name them by touch, eyes shut.

text: The workshop manager ran through the order of operations before the run began. The pieces are cut first, he said, on cloth laid perfectly flat and along the grain, or the jacket will twist the first time it is washed. The woman in charge of cutting replied that the pattern had been checked the day before and that the templates were sound. He went on: the shoulders are joined next, the sleeves are set in after that, and only then does the lining go in. One of the operators asked whether the lining should be clipped in place before stitching. The answer came back flat. Clip it, check that it hangs true, then stitch. The fastening comes last of all. Before anything leaves the workshop, the cutter added, the garment is done up on a dummy, because a misalignment shows on the stand and can still be put right.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)

text: Colour once cost more than the cloth it was laid on, and that oddity weighed on the whole history of dress. Lasting pigments came from shellfish, from insects, from uncommon roots, and each of them yielded only a meagre harvest. Scarcity turned into a visible ranking, since you could read a household's standing in the depth of its reds and purples. The authorities widened the gap further by barring certain shades to the lower orders. Unable to dye within the law, humble workshops fell back on greys, browns and undyed cloth, which fixed for generations the notion that ordinary dress was drab. Then dyes drawn from a by-product of industry overturned the arrangement altogether. Once bright colour came within reach of every purse, it no longer marked out wealth, and the cut of a garment took over that office.

text: A jumper straight out of the shop soon covers itself in tiny balls of fibre, and that wear puts off whoever has only just bought it. The cause is mechanical: short fibre ends work their way to the surface under rubbing, tangle together, then build into little knots that catch the eye. Yarns spun from long, well-combed fibres slide over one another and pill far less. The first move therefore comes at the counter, where a dense, smooth knit is worth more than a fluffy one. After that, care counts as much as the material does. Washing inside a mesh bag, with no violent spin, cuts down the friction that tears fibres loose. And when knots do appear, a fabric shaver lifts them away cleanly, provided the garment is stretched flat and never pulled. The knit looks crisp again afterwards, and the treatment can be repeated without harm.

units: a woman living on the floor above owned two outdoor garments

text: The woman upstairs kept two coats in one wardrobe, and one evening she explained the difference to me. The first, thick and cut from felted woollen cloth, sat on the shoulders like a suit of armour. The second, made of oiled canvas, weighed almost nothing and folded away into a bag. She took the heavy one out when the wind bit, the light one when the rain came straight down. I wanted to settle the matter and crown one of them the better coat, and I was wrong. Caught in a downpour, I borrowed the woollen coat, and it drank the water like a sponge. Drying it out took two evenings. The other, for its part, left my back frozen the moment the cold set in. Now I stand at the wardrobe and choose by the look of the sky rather than by my own liking. Learning the hard way, my neighbour called it.

text: Here is the method that professional pressers recommend for taking the creases out of a shirt without scorching it. For kit, you want a padded board, an iron with a clean plate and a spray bottle of clear water within reach. For preparation, empty the pockets, unfasten the collar and damp the cloth lightly until it turns soft under the fingers. For order of work, begin at the collar, move on to the cuffs, then the sleeves, and finish with the back and the fronts, because narrow areas come before broad ones and large panels crumple last. For heat, set the iron to suit the most delicate fibre anywhere in the garment, and test it on a hidden seam first. For putting away, let the shirt cool on a hanger before you do it up, or the damp trapped inside will press in fresh creases.

text: The shed smelled of damp wool as the doors slid open, a little before dawn. The shearers had come the evening before, and the fleeces lay heaped in downy piles along the wall. In the first hour a sorter picked out the soiled locks, one after another, without lifting her head. Around the middle of the session the pressed bales went off to be washed, where warm water carried the grease away. Later the dried fibre passed through the carding machine, and the white cloud it threw off set the visitors coughing. At the end of the line a worker knitted a sample in front of the onlookers, using the first yarn to come off the frame. The cooperative hopes to revive a trade that buying from abroad had killed off. Nothing is settled yet: orders are still thin, and the shearers are growing old.
